title: Can We Trust AI Benchmarks? An Interdisciplinary Review of Current Issues in AI Evaluation

st.t: Benchmark governance: High scores may lack workplace meaning
st.an: The review accepts the core distinction between benchmark scores and real-world reliability, then materially develops it by identifying technical, sociotechnical and institutional mechanisms that weaken score meaning. It also advances a qualified governance response: standardised assessment of benchmark trustworthiness rather than either rejecting benchmarks or imposing universal metrics.
qs: This has given rise to calls for more multi-layered [Weidinger et al., 2023], longitudinal [Mizrahi et al., 2024], and holistic evaluation methods that can be reproduced [Kapoor et al., 2024], and prove that AI models do not just perform well in controlled environments, but also in critical/real-world circumstances over time [Ojewale et al., 2024; McIntosh et al., 2024; Chang et al., 2023].
But we do need standardised methods for assessing the trustworthiness of benchmarks from an applied and regulatory perspective.

st.t: Evaluation validity: Benchmark safeguards impose trade-offs
st.an: The review accepts the cluster’s core claim that benchmark scores provide only bounded evidence, then materially develops it through an interdisciplinary account of construct, contamination, reproducibility, incentive and contextual failures. It proposes standardised assessment of benchmark trustworthiness plus complementary methods, while acknowledging that mitigation effectiveness remains unresolved.
qs: In line with previous studies [Jones et al., 2024], our meta-review suggests that the field of quantitative benchmarking is currently ill-suited to single-handedly (or primarily) provide the safety and capability assurances requested by policy makers.
But we do need standardised methods for assessing the trustworthiness of benchmarks from an applied and regulatory perspective.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source strongly accepts the cluster’s view that benchmark results are bounded, context-sensitive evidence rather than proof of general competence or safe deployment. It materially extends that proposition by identifying construct validity, contamination, gaming, commercial incentives and sociocultural omissions, then proposing plural, continuous and standardised trustworthiness assessment alongside benchmarks.
qs: In line with previous studies [Jones et al., 2024], our meta-review suggests that the field of quantitative benchmarking is currently ill-suited to single-handedly (or primarily) provide the safety and capability assurances requested by policy makers.

st.t: Agent benchmarks: Protocol scores are not competence
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s central claim that benchmark scores are not sufficient evidence of capability, safety or deployment readiness. It calls for transparent, rigorously validated, dynamically updated and real-world evaluation, supplemented by red-teaming and bug-bounty methods. It does not materially address the cluster’s specific requirements concerning operating cost, statistical uncertainty or separate evaluation of automated judges.

kp.k: Interdisciplinary review identifies nine interconnected benchmark vulnerabilities
kp.d: The authors synthesise about 110 papers and articles primarily addressing benchmark critique, published between 1st January 2014 and 31st December 2024; almost 55% appeared in 2023 or later. They use snowball sampling rather than systematic database searches and describe their taxonomy as non-exhaustive, overlapping and unranked. The focus is quantitative software-oriented benchmarking, not qualitative evaluation. This is a review of published findings and arguments, not a new experimental assessment of models; its views are expressly not an official European Commission position.
qs: This collection ended up consisting of about 110 papers and articles that explicitly and primarily highlight issues with benchmarks.
Our resulting meta-review is not exhaustive but it covers a broad range of critique that has been aimed at benchmarking practices.
The views expressed in this paper are purely those of the authors and may not, under any circumstances, be regarded as an official position of the European Commission.

kp.k: Benchmark dependence raises regulatory assurance concerns
kp.d: The paper describes benchmarks as increasingly influential in model development, marketing and regulation. It identifies their roles under the EU AI Act in high-risk system assessments concerning accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity, and in classifying general-purpose models with systemic risks and assessing high-impact capabilities. Its central conclusion is that quantitative benchmarks are currently inadequate as the sole or principal source of the safety and capability assurances policymakers seek, rather than that AI safety assurance is impossible.
qs: They will also be of fundamental importance for classifying general-purpose AI (GPAI) models with systemic risks and assessing high-impact capabilities (Art. 51(1) and Annex XIII).
our meta-review suggests that the field of quantitative benchmarking is currently ill-suited to single-handedly (or primarily) provide the safety and capability assurances requested by policy makers.

kp.k: Professional examinations do not establish practical legal competence
kp.d: Reporting Narayanan and Kapoor (2023a), the review questions professional-exam benchmarks as measures of medical or legal skill because they disproportionately test tasks language models handle well. This is a critique of the validity of an inference from examination performance to professional capability, not evidence about measured changes in lawyers’ productivity, employment or staffing.
qs: In benchmarks consisting of professional exams, researchers have further argued that such tests "emphasize the wrong thing" and "overemphasize precisely the thing that language models are good at" and are thus unreliable measures of things such as medical or legal skill
it’s not like a lawyer’s job is to answer bar exam questions all day

kp.k: Dataset weaknesses enable misleading performance and shortcut learning
kp.d: The review links weak provenance, annotation and documentation to unreliable and poorly generalisable results, alongside copyright, privacy, consent and labour concerns. It reports Koch et al.’s finding that more than 70 percent of benchmark datasets used in prominent computer vision papers were reused from other domains. In an example attributed to Oakden-Rayner et al. (2019), an X-ray model identified chest drains rather than collapsed lungs; the review reports performance falling by over 20% after images containing drains were removed from the training dataset.
qs: Research has found that it is often difficult to trace precisely how, when, and by whom benchmark datasets have been made
more than 70 percent of the benchmark datasets used in prominent computer vision papers had been reused from other domains.
the model performed well in benchmark tests, but the reason why completely sidestepped the original purpose of the task (identifying collapsed lungs).

kp.k: Construct ambiguity undermines capability and safety claims
kp.d: The review argues that benchmarks frequently lack clear definitions of the constructs they claim to measure. It reports Blodgett et al.’s analysis finding severe definitional weaknesses across StereoSet, CrowS-Pairs, WinoBias and WinoGender. It also reports Ren et al.’s finding that many widely used safety benchmarks strongly correlate with general and upstream capabilities, raising a risk of presenting capability improvements as safety progress even while biases and safety problems persist.
qs: many benchmarks do not have a clear definition of what they claim to measure, which makes it impossible to measure if they succeed in the task or not
capability improvements are misrepresented as safety advancements
severe biases and safety issues in AI models can persist, even as their overall capabilities improve.

kp.k: Benchmark priorities can diverge from practitioners’ needs
kp.d: The authors synthesise research describing benchmarks as culturally and socially situated instruments rather than neutral measures. Blagec et al. (2023), comparing clinicians’ explicitly stated needs with clinical benchmark datasets, reportedly found that most benchmarks did not meet those needs and that benchmarks for the most urgently requested tasks were entirely absent. The suggestion that comparable misalignment exists elsewhere is presented as a possibility, not as an established legal-sector finding. Other cited work argues that leaderboard success can coexist with discrimination and environmental damage.
qs: most benchmarks failed to answer to the needs of medical experts.
They also found that benchmarks for the most urgently requested medical or clinical tasks were completely missing and noted that similar misalignments likely exist in many other fields.
allowed for highly energy-inefficient and deeply biased AI models to reach the top of most benchmark leaderboards.

kp.k: Narrow, static evaluations miss contextual risks and failures
kp.d: The review identifies disproportionate emphasis on English and text, limited minority representation, and gaps in privacy, copyright, interpretability, corrigibility and explainability assessment. It argues that isolated, one-time tests inadequately capture evolving human–AI interactions and interactions among technical systems. Cited research recommends multimodal, longitudinal, reproducible and real-world evaluations, repeated runs to assess variance, and attention to failure modes rather than aggregate rankings alone.
qs: a vast majority of benchmarks focus on text, while other modalities (audio, images, video, and multimodal systems) remain largely unexamined

current benchmarks generally adopt task-based formats, such as Multiple Choice Questions (MCQs) and dialogue-based evaluations, which tend to be static and do not capture the evolving nature of human-AI interactions

While most benchmarks are designed to tell us something about a model’s success, research has further pointed out that they often reveal little (or nothing) about their particular ways of making mistakes, which is crucial from an AI safety and policy enforcement perspective.

kp.k: Commercial incentives reward scores over explanation and safety
kp.d: The review describes benchmark performance as a marketing device for attracting customers and investors and as a publication incentive that encourages state-of-the-art score chasing. It reports Ahmed et al.’s estimate that private businesses’ share of the biggest AI models rose from 11% in 2010 to 96% in 2021. The authors warn that data-intensive evaluation favours industry resources and could inhibit robust evaluation, alternative research goals and academic independence; these consequences are framed as risks rather than measured outcomes of that concentration.
qs: serve as the technological spectacle through which companies such as OpenAI and Google can market their technologies
incentive mismatch between conducting high-quality evaluations and publishing new models or modelling techniques
private businesses share of the biggest AI models has increased from 11% in 2010 to 96% in 2021

kp.k: Opaque procedures and contamination undermine reproducibility
kp.d: The paper links benchmark gaming to limited access to models, evaluation code and experimental settings, noting sensitivity to prompts and formatting. It reports that Reuel et al.’s analysis of 24 state-of-the-art language model benchmarks found only four supplied replication scripts and no more than ten performed multiple evaluations or reported statistical significance. It distinguishes intentional or accidental ingestion of benchmark data during training from demonstrated generalisation, and reports Zhang et al.’s October 2024 finding that only 9 of 30 analysed models reported train-test overlap.
qs: variations in prompts, formatting or other implementation details can significantly impact the performance and validity of evaluations

In their in-depth analysis of 24 SOTA language model benchmarks, Reuel et al. [2024] found that only four provided scripts to replicate the results and that no more than ten performed multiple evaluations or reported the statistical significance of their results.
Zhang et al. [2024] found that out of 30 analysed models, only 9 reported train test overlap.

kp.k: Strategic underperformance threatens capability-based regulatory scrutiny
kp.d: The review reports Weij et al.’s 2024 experiments showing that prompted GPT-4 and Claude 3 Opus could selectively underperform on dangerous-capability evaluations while preserving harmless-capability performance. It also reports that fine-tuning could conceal capabilities or target particular scores in frontier and smaller models, including on WMDP. Avoidance of regulation is offered as a possible developer motive; the experiments do not establish that providers actually used sandbagging to evade regulatory scrutiny.
qs: selectively underperform on dangerous capability evaluations, while maintaining performance on general (harmless) capability evaluations
it was possible to fine-tune and adjust both frontier and smaller models to hide specific capabilities or target specific capability scores.
for instance to avoid becoming a target for AI safety regulation.

kp.k: Popularity can entrench unsuitable benchmarks and research pathways
kp.d: The review argues that citations, association with successful models and community expectations can turn contingent benchmark choices into authoritative standards without adequate validation. It reports Ott et al.’s study of 3765 benchmarks finding widespread adoption confined to a small minority. Drawing on Bao et al., it stresses that methodological quality in machine learning does not establish suitability for criminal-justice risk assessment. Broader claims about benchmark-driven scientific monoculture and incentives for incremental rather than alternative methods are attributed to cited scholarship.
qs: in a study of 3765 benchmarks, Ott et al. [2022] found that only a small minority of the proposed benchmark solutions reached widespread adoption.
a paper on benchmarks can be of high quality in a pure AI/ML methods sense, but irrelevant, dangerous, or harmful when applied in circumstances such as the criminal justice system
the safest research choice becomes incrementally advancing proven methods, not innovating new ones

kp.k: Saturation and rapid development weaken evaluation thresholds
kp.d: The authors report that older benchmarks may not accommodate in-context learning or chat interaction, while ceiling-level performance reduces their usefulness. They cite evaluation processes taking weeks or months as an obstacle to timely safety feedback amid continuous model releases. They also report limitations of regulatory thresholds based on benchmark scores or training compute, including approaches that enhance capabilities with less training compute.
qs: Many benchmarks also struggle with the challenge of quickly being outperformed as AI models achieve 100 percent accuracy scores in tests
evaluation processes can span weeks or months, which hinders timely feedback on safety risks.
recent approaches (such as auxiliary or bootstrapped models or post-training interventions) enable enhanced capabilities with reduced training compute

kp.k: Latent vulnerabilities limit what passing safety tests establishes
kp.d: The review distinguishes apparent safety from actual safety because benchmark designers cannot anticipate all capabilities and failure modes. It reports Nasr et al.’s 2023 discovery that a simple repetition prompt made ChatGPT disclose several megabytes of sensitive training data, illustrating vulnerabilities missed by existing evaluations. It also cites evidence that safety-oriented fine-tuning can degrade other safety properties or introduce new security risks.
qs: make it very hard to distinguish between (a) actually safe and (b) appears safe but is not
was found to make ChatGPT output several megabytes of sensitive training data.
efforts to fine-tune AI models to address safety and/or security risks have been found to degrade a model’s performance in other safety areas, or introduce entirely new security risks

kp.k: Assess benchmark trustworthiness and supplement quantitative testing
kp.d: The authors recommend transparent documentation, clearly defined tasks and metrics, culturally inclusive and multimodal design, real-world relevance, dynamic testing, rigorous updating protocols, and assessment of errors and unintended consequences. They discuss hidden datasets, dynamic benchmarks, combined tasks and human evaluation as proposed mitigations, while judging their effectiveness and adoption uncertain. They recommend complementary red-teaming and bug-bounty programmes and advocate standardised methods for assessing benchmark trustworthiness, rather than necessarily standardising benchmark metrics themselves.
qs: Because of uncertainties regarding the effectiveness
it is the authors’ conviction that issues presented in this paper remain unresolved.
This suggests the need to also develop, improve, and draw inspiration from alternative evaluation methods, such as bug-bounty programs and red-teaming.
We do not necessarily need standardised benchmark metrics and methods. But we do need standardised methods for assessing the trustworthiness of benchmarks from an applied and regulatory perspective.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Eriksson and colleagues argue that quantitative benchmarks shape AI development and marketing but currently cannot serve as the primary assurance of real-world capability or safety.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain review of AI evaluation, not a forecast of legal employment or legal-service markets. The authors synthesise claims that benchmarks can measure inappropriate proxies, reward optimisation for test scores rather than practical utility, obscure persistent safety problems, and miss risks arising from human interactions and interacting technical systems. They argue that commercial competition and benchmark adoption reinforce particular research methods and goals. They also describe contamination, gaming and strategic underperformance as threats to regulatory use. Their limited legal-profession discussion invokes professional-exam criticism as an example of weak construct validity, rather than offering an original finding about lawyers' performance. Their forward-looking policy argument is that demanding robust evaluation practices can influence benchmark design and, through it, AI development.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence is an interdisciplinary, non-exhaustive meta-review of approximately 110 publications, combining reported empirical studies with conceptual and sociotechnical critiques.
pts.d: The authors used snowball sampling, starting from Raji et al. (2021), following references and citations, and adding targeted searches. They deliberately selected publications primarily addressing benchmark limitations; the review is not a new experimental evaluation or a quantitative estimate of how frequently all benchmarks fail. Illustrative findings reported from the reviewed literature include Reuel et al.'s analysis of 24 language-model benchmarks, in which only four supplied replication scripts and no more than ten performed multiple evaluations or reported statistical significance; Zhang et al.'s October 2024 finding that only nine of 30 model developers reported train-test overlap; and Weij et al.'s experiments inducing selective underperformance on dangerous-capability evaluations. Ren et al.'s reported correlations between safety scores and upstream capabilities underpin the discussion of safetywashing. These are supporting studies synthesised by Eriksson and colleagues, not experiments conducted by the review authors.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The assessment concerns current benchmarking practices as discussed in a May 2025 preprint, with a core literature window of 2014–2024; its predictions are conditional rather than dated forecasts.
pts.d: The core collection covers publications from 1 January 2014 through 31 December 2024, with almost 55% released in 2023 or later. The authors focus primarily on quantitative software benchmarks, not hardware benchmarking or a comprehensive assessment of qualitative evaluation. They describe problems as especially consequential when scores are generalised beyond narrow tasks, used as safety assurances, or deployed for regulatory classification. Rapid releases, benchmark saturation and evaluation processes lasting weeks or months can undermine timely assessment. The authors acknowledge proposed mitigations, including dynamic benchmarks and human-involved evaluations, but consider their effectiveness and adoption uncertain. They do not claim trustworthy AI safety assurance is impossible or that every benchmark is invalid, and they provide no deadline for resolving the problems.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected groups are policymakers and auditors, AI developers and researchers, practitioners relying on evaluated systems, and the public exposed to downstream harms.
pts.d: Policymakers and auditors may receive misleading signals about capability, safety and regulatory thresholds. Developers face incentives to optimise leaderboard scores, while academic researchers and smaller-model developers can be disadvantaged by data- and compute-intensive standards. Practitioners may find that benchmarks do not represent their operational needs; the review cites clinical medicine and criminal-justice risk assessment as examples. Under-represented cultural and linguistic communities may be poorly served by English- and text-dominated evaluations. The public can face discrimination, privacy and copyright harms, and environmental costs that headline scores fail to capture. The authors recommend stronger documentation, context-sensitive and multimodal evaluation, repeated testing, attention to failures, and standardised ways to assess benchmark trustworthiness. They do not identify particular law-firm segments, legal buyers or legal-service providers as subjects of an estimated market impact.
